analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal rules requiring Americans to report offshore accounts and foreign income.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have dismantled the reporting and penalty rules for Americans' foreign accounts, died without a hearing or vote after being referred to the House Ways and Means Committee with 4 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill repeals the core enforcement rules behind the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA), a 2010 law that requires Americans with overseas accounts to report them, requires foreign banks to tell the IRS about American account holders, and penalizes taxpayers who hide foreign income. The bill would eliminate those reporting requirements, the penalties for failing to disclose foreign assets, and the extended time limit the IRS has to audit hidden foreign income. Supporters called the rules burdensome and an intrusion on foreign nations' sovereignty and financial privacy.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy Americans with undisclosed foreign accounts gain the most: they would no longer have to report foreign assets on Form 8938, would escape the enhanced penalties for hiding foreign income, and the IRS would lose its extended six-year window to audit large unreported income. Foreign banks and offshore financial firms also gain, since FATCA made them report American account holders and withhold taxes in some cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Holders of offshore accounts and foreign banks

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the requirement that U.S. taxpayers report specified foreign financial assets (section 6038D), eliminating the Form 8938 filing for offshore accounts.
Repeals the extra 40% penalty on underpaid tax attributable to undisclosed foreign financial assets and the enhanced penalties for failing to report foreign trusts.

Repeals the withholding requirements imposed on payments to foreign financial institutions and other foreign entities that do not comply, the compliance obligation that caused many foreign banks to drop American clients.
Restores the standard statute of limitations, striking the extended six-year rule for significant omissions of income connected to foreign assets.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers generally, because the offshore reporting regime exists to catch income hidden abroad; repealing it would reduce the taxes collected from people with hidden foreign accounts, shifting more of the burden onto everyone else and weakening IRS enforcement capacity.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating reporting and penalties for undisclosed foreign assets would make it easier to hide income offshore, reducing tax revenue that ordinary taxpayers would otherwise not have to make up.
The bill removes the extended audit window for large unreported foreign income, limiting the IRS's ability to pursue substantial evasion discovered after the normal three-year period.
Supporters' own framing concedes the cost: the appeal rests on compliance burdens and privacy concerns, not on any finding that the offshore reporting rules fail to raise revenue or catch evasion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to a narrow group — people with foreign assets and institutions that service them — in the form of lower compliance costs and weaker enforcement against hidden offshore income, while the cost is spread across all taxpayers. There is no mechanism in the bill to replace the revenue or enforcement that would be lost.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in September 2016, it was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Meadows introduced the bill on September 6, 2016, joined by Reps. Mulvaney and Duncan of South Carolina, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill attracted 4 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no further action of any kind appears in its record.
The House adjourned for the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the FATCA reporting and penalty rules stayed in place; the main beneficiaries of its defeat are the IRS's offshore enforcement program and taxpayers who do not hide income abroad. No industry gained from the bill's passage because it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore enforcement stayed intact; ordinary taxpayers

for.name: Rep. Mark Meadows
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal FATCA's withholding, reporting, and penalty provisions.

for.name: Reps. Mick Mulvaney and Jeff Duncan
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All 5 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill and no committee or floor vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Offshore financial services and foreign banks
industries.note: FATCA requires foreign financial institutions to report American account holders and imposes withholding on noncompliant institutions, a costly compliance burden that led many foreign banks to close American accounts. Repeal would free them of that burden at the cost of transparency that helps catch offshore tax evasion.

industries.industry: Wealthy households with undisclosed foreign assets
industries.note: The bill eliminates asset reporting, the 40% penalty on hidden foreign income, and the extended audit window — the specific enforcement tools aimed at offshore evasion. Its gain comes directly from weakened enforcement that ordinary taxpayers fund.
